pr_title: Fix AccessViolation/InvalidProgramException in custom nullable converters.
pr_body:
Fixes a condition where a custom nullable type converter can result in `AccessViolationException`/`InvalidProgramExceptions` when the user has opted into the underlying struct type via `CanConvert` overrides.

We already have logic for detecting the converse, namely struct converters opting into nullable converters, so this PR is merely extending the existing checks.

Fixes #55135.

> Should this be an || here?

I think that this check is intentional, apparently it is meant to support "covariant" and "contravariant" converters and will only fail if there is no subtype relationship between the two types. Here are some tests that validate this:

https://github.com/dotnet/runtime/blob/a8dacd5577b4da88555f342abc8d5a3f219edca0/src/libraries/System.Text.Json/tests/System.Text.Json.Tests/Serialization/CustomConverterTests/CustomConverterTests.BadConverters.cs#L46-L57

I find that this mode is flawed since serialization is contravariant and deserialization is covariant, meaning that covariant serialization and contravariant deserialization will necessarily manifest as various kinds of runtime type errors. On top of that, much of the serialization infrastructure is built on the assumption that `JsonConverter<T>` is invariant, see for example:

* [IEnumerableDefaultConverter](https://github.com/dotnet/runtime/blob/a036594cb3766f70db9f5c6e7681454e6894da50/src/libraries/System.Text.Json/src/System/Text/Json/Serialization/Converters/Collection/IEnumerableDefaultConverter.cs#L22)
* [DictionaryDefaultConverter](https://github.com/dotnet/runtime/blob/a036594cb3766f70db9f5c6e7681454e6894da50/src/libraries/System.Text.Json/src/System/Text/Json/Serialization/Converters/Collection/DictionaryDefaultConverter.cs#L43)
* [JsonPropertyInfoOfT](https://github.com/dotnet/runtime/blob/a036594cb3766f70db9f5c6e7681454e6894da50/src/libraries/System.Text.Json/src/System/Text/Json/Serialization/Metadata/JsonPropertyInfoOfT.cs#L225)
* [ObjectWithParameterizedConstructorConverter](https://github.com/dotnet/runtime/blob/a036594cb3766f70db9f5c6e7681454e6894da50/src/libraries/System.Text.Json/src/System/Text/Json/Serialization/Converters/Object/ObjectWithParameterizedConstructorConverter.Small.cs#L66)

and therefore any "contraviariant"/"covariant" converter will necessarily manifest as an `InvalidCastException` when composed with collection converters or constructor arguments.

Ultimately, that is the root cause for the reported issue: `JsonPropertyInfo` instances are [constructed based on the converter type](https://github.com/dotnet/runtime/blob/a8dacd5577b4da88555f342abc8d5a3f219edca0/src/libraries/System.Text.Json/src/System/Text/Json/Serialization/JsonConverterOfT.cs#L59) and not the `PropertyInfo` type. This in turn results in us [emitting dynamic method accessors that contain type errors](https://github.com/dotnet/runtime/blob/a8dacd5577b4da88555f342abc8d5a3f219edca0/src/libraries/System.Text.Json/src/System/Text/Json/Serialization/Metadata/JsonPropertyInfoOfT.cs#L68), which causes the `AccessViolationException`.

One was of addressing this issue as well as #46522 is to force converter invariance everywhere, namely changing the check in [`GetConverterInternal`](https://github.com/dotnet/runtime/blob/90b8ddd7a6b28e57aebed7d478547ce07b9b60a6/src/libraries/System.Text.Json/src/System/Text/Json/Serialization/JsonSerializerOptions.Converters.cs#L253-L257) to say
```csharp

            if (converter.TypeToConvert != typeToConvert)
            {
                ThrowHelper.ThrowInvalidOperationException_SerializationConverterNotCompatible(converter.GetType(), typeToConvert);
            }
```
This will ensure consistent behavior across the board (regardless of whether the converter is used as a root-level object or collection element) and any type mismatches will manifest as the same user-friendly error messages occurring early in the serialization process. Perhaps something to consider for .NET 7.

@layomia @steveharter @ericstj thoughts?

We should not be causing AccessViolation. Ideally we improve the error detection upfront. If that is not feasible, we could add some `castclass` opcodes in the IL generation that will throw `InvalidCastException`, but that will have a small impact on runtime perf.

The converter model was not intended to be covariant - the JsonConverterFactory should be used to instantiate the correct converter.
This could be moved to 7.0; I don't believe the semantics changed in 6.0.
I already have a PR open that fixes this: #56577

review_comments:
I think it's better to disallow it as done in this PR and have users provide converter implementations that align with what we intend. This way we can keep IL logic as simplified as possible and reduce the possibility of type errors.

- use a `JsonConverter<double>` if you want custom support for `double` and `double?` (supported by the serializer wrapping custom converter in `NullableConverter<>`)
- use a `JsonConverter<double?>` if you want custom support for `double?` specifically (for whatever reason). A separate `JsonConverter<double>` will be needed for `double` support in this case.
With your fix, do we still have coverage for this branch? Same question for the location of the new debug assert below.
Yeah, they're both covered by the new tests I added.

@layomia @steveharter Based on the comments above I _think_ that this check should use `IsNullableOfT()` which is what the original PR adding this check was doing: https://github.com/dotnet/runtime/commit/99829d5017b274537ada263ea7002ec576fa85d5

My feeling is it got changed accidentally to `CanBeNull()` during a refactoring.
nit: can we have comments or update the test method and/or test type names to indicate whey the converters are "bad"? (Faulty `CanConvert(Type)` implementations...)
